hook.text: JavaScript makes the web interactive. The engine is the brain that runs it — fast, compiled, and optimized.

buildup.text: V8 (Chrome), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), and JavaScriptCore (Safari) compile JS to machine code at runtime.

discovery.text: JIT compilation profiles hot code paths and optimizes them. Cold paths run interpreted for quick startup.

twist.text: Garbage collection reclaims unused memory. Pauses used to freeze pages. Modern GCs work incrementally.

climax.text: V8 powers Node.js too. The same engine that runs your browser also runs server-side JavaScript.

punchline.text: JS engines JIT-compile code at runtime. Fast enough for apps.

quiz.question: What technique do modern JS engines use to maximize performance?
options: JIT compilation that optimizes hot code paths
Pre-compiling all JavaScript before the page loads
Running JavaScript in a separate thread by default

details.summary: JavaScript engines like V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore compile and execute JavaScript code in browsers. V8 uses just-in-time compilation to translate JavaScript to optimized machine code at runtime, achieving performance that approaches compiled languages for many workloads.
details.whyItMatters: JavaScript engines determine the performance of every web application. Understanding their optimization strategies helps developers write code that runs faster in the browser.
takeaways: JIT compilation converts JavaScript to optimized machine code at runtime
V8 powers Chrome, Node.js, and Deno with high performance
Hidden classes and inline caching optimize property access speed

faq.question: How does just-in-time compilation work?
faq.answer: JIT compilers monitor which code runs frequently and compile it to optimized machine code. Cold code is interpreted quickly. Hot code is compiled with optimizations based on observed types and patterns.

faq.question: Why are there multiple JavaScript engines?
faq.answer: Each browser vendor builds their own engine: V8 for Chrome, SpiderMonkey for Firefox, JavaScriptCore for Safari. Competition drives performance improvements. They all implement the same ECMAScript standard but differ in optimization strategies.
